text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the July 24 editions of Russian newspapers. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- A decision by Russia's Gazprom natural gas monopoly to cut the amount of gas delivered to debt-ridden Belarus and Ukraine shows that the company may be moving away from political considerations in its business strategy.
- Russia's Atomic Energy ministry considers boosting uranium sales a top priority while its U.S. counterpart is more concerned about strict controls over such exports.
- President Yeltsin has reserved for himself the ultimate right to decide who among the many refugees coming to Russia should be granted political immigrant status.

- Alexander Pochinok, head of the tax service and shareholder in Mechel metals smelter, has promised tough measures against the company, as well as a number of other tax-dodgers, if they do not pay all their debts to the budget.
- The first Hi-Ace commercial vehicles the Japaneese automaker Toyota is planning to assemble in Russia could leave the factory as early as 1999.
- Russia urgently needs a law on prevention of mafia infiltration into the banking system.
- The idea to send Russian state officers abroad for training will yield fruit only if those chosen for the scheme are truly bright and talented.

- Coordinated work by the executive branch of power and the legislators should make it possible to quickly overcome the many shortcomings of the law on religious organisations in Russia which prompted President Yeltsin to turn it down.
- President Yeltsin's choice of the Northern Russian republic of Karelia as his holiday destination could give a boost to the tourist sector of the region's crisis-stricken economy.

- The Russian Orthodox Church has urged President Yeltsin to be swift in signing the law on religious organisations in Russia but the sphere of confessional freedom is exactly that part of public life where one has to think twice before making a decision.
- A shot fired at the apartment of Central Bank chairman Sergei Dubinin could mark an intensification of turf battles in Russia's banking sector.
- A tax of about $10 will be levied on everyone crossing the Russian border.
